name: Myasthenic crisis

matching.reasoningTemplate: Fatigable weakness with diplopia and respiratory compromise suggests a myasthenic crisis.

redFlags: Bulbar/respiratory weakness — airway support; avoid precipitating drugs

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e, Chapter 459 (Myasthenia Gravis and Other Diseases of the Neuromuscular Junction), p.3624-3633
clinicalPearls: Myasthenic crisis is an exacerbation of weakness severe enough to endanger life, typically with ventilatory failure from diaphragmatic and intercostal muscle weakness; by definition, ventilatory weakness requiring intubation or noninvasive ventilation to avoid intubation constitutes crisis, whereas lesser worsening is termed exacerbation (p.3625, 3632).
Weakness is characteristically fatigable: it worsens with repeated use and late in the day and improves with rest or sleep, and strength can improve with serial effort (contrast with LEMS) (p.3625).

Cranial muscles are often involved early, with diplopia and ptosis common initial symptoms; facial weakness gives a 'snarling' expression on attempted smile, and bulbar involvement causes nasal/'mushy' dysarthria, hoarseness, and dysphagia with risk of nasal regurgitation or aspiration (p.3625).
Bulbar, neck, and ventilatory weakness can be especially prominent in MuSK antibody-positive MG; neck extensor weakness can cause head drop (p.3625).
Deep tendon reflexes are typically preserved and sensory symptoms, sensory loss, and pain are absent in MG (p.3625).

Anti-AChR antibodies are present in ~85% of generalized MG and ~50% of ocular MG; a positive test is virtually diagnostic, but a negative test does not exclude MG, and antibody level does not correlate well with severity (p.3627).
About 10% of MG patients (~40% of AChR-negative generalized MG) have anti-MuSK antibodies, and 1-3% have anti-LRP4; ~10% of generalized MG is double-seronegative (p.3625, 3627).
The ice-pack test (ice over a ptotic lid for 2 min, positive if lid rises >=2 mm) is a quick, very sensitive bedside test for an NMJ cause of ptosis (p.3627).
Edrophonium (anticholinesterase) testing was historically used for diagnosis but is no longer used due to side effects and lack of availability (p.3627).

Thymic abnormality occurs in ~75% of AChR-positive patients; thymoma is present in ~10-15% of MG patients, so chest CT/MRI is performed at diagnosis (thymic enlargement in a patient >40 years is highly suspicious for thymoma) (p.3625, 3630).
harrison.pathophysiology: MG is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder in which the number of available postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) is reduced and postsynaptic folds are flattened/simplified, decreasing the efficiency of neuromuscular transmission; ACh is released normally but produces small end-plate potentials that may fail to trigger muscle action potentials. The normal decline in ACh release on repeated activity (presynaptic rundown) combined with reduced transmission efficiency activates fewer fibers with successive impulses, producing fatigable weakness (myasthenic fatigue) and the decremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation. Anti-AChR antibodies (IgG, T-cell dependent) reduce receptors by three mechanisms: accelerated AChR turnover via cross-linking/endocytosis, complement-mediated damage to the postsynaptic membrane, and blockade of the ACh-binding site. Anti-MuSK antibodies (IgG4, non-complement-activating) impair MuSK-LRP4 binding and AChR clustering, so MuSK-positive MG does not respond to complement inhibition; anti-LRP4 antibodies (IgG1) cause complement-mediated destruction. Thymic abnormality (hyperplasia in ~65%, thymoma in ~10%) and dysfunction of regulatory T cells contribute to the autoimmune process (p.3624-3626).
additionalDifferentials: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS): presynaptic P/Q-type calcium-channel antibody disorder; proximal lower-limb weakness predominates, reflexes are depressed/absent, autonomic features (dry mouth, orthostasis, impotence) occur, and an incremental response follows high-rate stimulation or brief exercise; associated with small-cell lung cancer in older adults (p.3628).
Congenital myasthenic syndromes (non-autoimmune, >30 genes; usually onset in infancy/childhood, AChR and MuSK antibodies absent) (p.3627-3628).
Drug-induced myasthenia, including penicillamine-associated MG and immune checkpoint inhibitor-related MG (p.3627, 3633).
Botulism (Clostridium botulinum toxin): myasthenia-like bulbar weakness with dilated/poorly reactive pupils and autonomic features; CMAP amplitudes increase after high-frequency stimulation (p.3628).
Hyperthyroidism/Graves disease and thyroid dysfunction, which can also aggravate myasthenic weakness (p.3627-3628, 3630).
Intracranial mass lesion compressing extraocular nerves (e.g., sphenoid ridge meningioma) causing diplopia (p.3628).
Oculopharyngeal dystrophy and progressive external ophthalmoplegia / mitochondrial myopathy (e.g., Kearns-Sayre) (p.3627-3628).
ICI-associated myositis (and myocarditis), which can mimic MG with ocular/bulbar weakness but without a decrementing response on repetitive nerve stimulation (p.3627, 3633).
nonInfectiousMimics: Cholinergic crisis from excessive anticholinesterase medication can mimic worsening MG; it is considered in the differential but is unlikely now because very high cholinesterase-inhibitor doses are rarely used (p.3632).
ICI-associated myositis can clinically resemble MG (prominent or exclusive ocular weakness) but lacks a decrementing response on repetitive nerve stimulation (p.3633).
additionalInvestigations: Repetitive nerve stimulation showing a decrement of >10% at 2-3 Hz in weak/proximal muscles supports MG; acetylcholinesterase inhibitors should be stopped 12-24 h beforehand (p.3627).
Single-fiber EMG (jitter and blocking with normal fiber density) when repetitive stimulation is normal or symptoms are exclusively ocular; confirmatory but not specific (p.3627).
Ice-pack test for improvement in ptosis (very sensitive) (p.3627).
Anti-MuSK and (if AChR/MuSK negative with clear MG phenotype) anti-LRP4 antibody testing (p.3627).
Chest CT or MRI to evaluate for thymoma/thymic abnormality at diagnosis (p.3627, 3630).

Thyroid function tests, antinuclear antibodies, and rheumatoid factor to detect associated/exacerbating conditions; testing for tuberculosis, fasting glucose/HbA1c, and bone densitometry before immunotherapy (p.3630).
MRI of the brain/orbits to exclude intracranial lesions in ocular or cranial presentations (p.3627-3628).
redFlags: Ventilatory failure from diaphragmatic/intercostal weakness is the life-threatening feature defining crisis; need for intubation or noninvasive ventilation to avoid intubation marks the transition from exacerbation to crisis (p.3625, 3632).

Intercurrent infection is the most common cause of crisis and must be treated immediately, as the patient's mechanical and immunologic defenses are compromised; fever with early infection should be managed as in an immunocompromised patient (p.3632).

Exposure to drugs that exacerbate weakness (e.g., aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, beta-blockers, magnesium, procainamide, quinine derivatives, neuromuscular blocking agents) can precipitate or worsen crisis (p.3633).
Tapering of MG therapies, unrelated infections, systemic disorders, or surgery can precipitate exacerbation or crisis; some exacerbations have no identifiable precipitant (p.3625).
Prominent bulbar/neck weakness (notably in MuSK-positive MG) signals aspiration and airway risk (p.3625).
harrison.prognosis: Mortality from MG has fallen dramatically over the last century (from ~70% a century ago to ~2-30% by the 1950s) to contemporary estimates of ~1-5%. About 20% of patients achieve sustained remission and can be tapered off immunotherapy, with no clear correlation between disease severity and likelihood of remission. Anti-MuSK MG was historically harder to treat, but rituximab has improved its prognosis. Most patients can be returned to full productive lives with proper therapy (p.3629, 3633).
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish myasthenic crisis from cholinergic crisis (deterioration due to excessive anticholinesterase medication); the latter is now unlikely because very high cholinesterase-inhibitor doses are rarely used but should still be considered (p.3632).

Treating before the diagnosis is confirmed: confirmation is essential because other treatable conditions closely resemble MG and treatment involves surgery and long-term drugs with side effects (p.3625).
Interpreting a negative anti-AChR antibody test as excluding MG, or using antibody level to gauge severity (it correlates poorly) (p.3627).
Overlooking that anti-MuSK MG generally responds poorly to anticholinesterase agents and may actually worsen with them (p.3629).
Ordering anti-striated muscle (titin) antibodies expecting them to confirm MG or thymoma: they are non-pathogenic and do not confirm either (p.3627).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison distinguishes ocular MG (weakness confined to ocular muscles; if restricted for 3 years, generalization is unlikely) from generalized MG (facial, bulbar, axial, or limb involvement, occurring in ~85%). Worsening is graded as exacerbation (any deterioration short of needing ventilatory support) versus myasthenic crisis (life-threatening weakness, usually with ventilatory failure requiring intubation or noninvasive ventilation to avoid intubation) (p.3625, 3632).
